paragraphs: Reconstructing a human body in three dimensions from one image can leave several answers consistent with the evidence. Occlusion makes this ambiguity more pronounced because parts of the body are hidden. This paper treats that uncertainty as part of the reconstruction problem: the goal is to produce several plausible bodies instead of committing to a single interpretation.

The method uses a neural network that predicts M candidate reconstructions and trains with a best-of-M loss. Body shape and pose are expressed through a suitable parametric 3D model, such as SMPL. A generative model also constrains each candidate to a space of plausible human poses, so producing multiple answers remains tied to realistic body configurations.

The authors report better ambiguous-pose recovery than alternative approaches on standard human reconstruction benchmarks and heavily occluded versions of those benchmarks. These findings support representing ambiguity explicitly through several constrained hypotheses. The contribution is a way to recover plausible alternatives when the image itself cannot uniquely determine the underlying body.
neurips-2020-3d-multi-bodies-fitting-set.tldr: A neural network predicts several plausible 3D human bodies to handle ambiguity and occlusion in single-image reconstruction.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search depends on how candidate networks are represented to the search algorithm. A common approach describes a network as a directed acyclic graph, then encodes its connections and operations as hyperparameters. This paper investigates why changing that encoding can substantially change search performance, even when architecture representation might appear to be an implementation detail.

The authors formally define architecture encodings and characterize the scalability of the encodings they study. They then identify the search subroutines whose behavior depends on these representations and experimentally examine which encodings work best with each subroutine across several popular algorithms.

This separation helps distinguish gains due to a search algorithm from gains due to its chosen encoding. The experiments therefore serve both as an ablation of earlier work and as guidance for designing future searches. The stated conclusion is that encoding deserves explicit attention as a consequential design choice: evaluating a NAS method requires considering how its representation interacts with the operations that drive the search.
neurips-2020-a-study-on-encodings-for-ne.tldr: A theoretical and empirical study shows that architecture encodings can substantially influence neural architecture search performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies online prediction when the quantity being tracked changes over time and feedback arrives through noisy gradients. Performance is measured by dynamic regret under squared error: how much the learner loses compared with a reference sequence that can itself change. The central question is how to exploit structure in that changing sequence.

The authors introduce a constraint based on discrete kth-order total variation, with radius C_n. This describes reference sequences with piecewise polynomial structure and controls their permitted variation. Drawing connections to wavelet methods in nonparametric regression, they construct an algorithm that runs in polynomial time.

The algorithm achieves nearly optimal dynamic regret of order n^(1/(2k+3)) C_n^(2/(2k+3)), up to logarithmic factors. It adapts to C_n without needing that radius in advance, so its guarantee responds to the sequence's variation without requiring that quantity as an input. The authors also establish minimax optimality for several other nonparametric families, extending the policy's theoretical usefulness beyond the initial variation-based formulation.
neurips-2020-adaptive-online-estimation-.tldr: A polynomial-time online algorithm tracks piecewise polynomial trends with nearly optimal regret while adapting to an unknown variation budget.

paragraphs: When a learning task has several objectives, a common shortcut combines them using fixed weights. A model can perform well on that combined score while performing poorly on individual objectives. The paper also points out that users' preferences may be unknown or difficult to express through one specific set of weights.

The proposed Agnostic Learning with Multiple Objectives framework optimizes for arbitrary mixture weights across the base objectives. Rather than treating a chosen mixture as the definitive target, it makes uncertainty about those weights part of the learning problem. The authors derive data-dependent Rademacher complexity guarantees and use them to guide both a scalable optimization algorithm and its regularization.

The algorithm has convergence guarantees when the loss functions and hypothesis space are convex. An implementation in a symbolic gradient computation framework is evaluated on several datasets, where the authors report benefits over learning with fixed mixture weights. The results support accounting explicitly for uncertainty in objective preferences, while the stated convergence result depends on the convexity assumptions.
neurips-2020-agnostic-learning-with-mult.tldr: The paper develops a learning framework that accounts for arbitrary mixtures of objectives instead of committing to fixed preference weights.

paragraphs: Panoptic segmentation combines identifying individual foreground objects with assigning background regions to semantic classes. Networks for this task contain several interacting components, including a backbone, separate foreground and background branches, and a feature fusion module. Designing these components together can require substantial expert effort and repeated trials.

Auto-Panoptic searches for all of these main components within a unified one-shot neural architecture search framework. It introduces search spaces for choices within modules and for relationships across modules. This makes the search sensitive both to the two segmentation tasks and to interactions between foreground objects and background classes.

To reduce the computational burden of searching such a complex system, the authors introduce a path-priority greedy search policy. They report substantially lower search overhead and a robust, transferable architecture. Auto-Panoptic achieves state-of-the-art results on COCO and ADE20K in the reported evaluation, with additional experiments supporting the search policy and transfer across datasets. The contribution links coordinated component design with a practical strategy for controlling search cost.
neurips-2020-auto-panoptic-cooperative-m.tldr: Auto-Panoptic jointly searches interacting segmentation components and uses a greedy search policy to reduce overhead while achieving strong benchmark results.

paragraphs: Classification can require optimizing more than the number of correct predictions. Measures such as F-measure or G-mean summarize different aspects of prediction quality, while requirements such as demographic parity or coverage constrain acceptable behavior. This paper addresses problems where both the objective and the constraints can be expressed as functions of a confusion matrix.

The method formulates optimization over matrices that satisfy two conditions: they can be achieved by a classifier, and they meet the problem's constraints. It reduces this optimization to a sequence of plug-in classifier learning problems. The resulting algorithm is statistically consistent, connecting this computational procedure to a learning guarantee.

When the objective and constraints are convex functions of the confusion matrix, the algorithm requires O(1/epsilon^2) calls to its plug-in routine, improving on the stated earlier O(1/epsilon^3) rate. This is a reduction in routine calls under the convexity condition. Empirically, the authors report performance at least as good as state-of-the-art methods for the examined constrained classification problems.
neurips-2020-consistent-plug-in-classifi.tldr: A consistent classifier-learning algorithm handles confusion-matrix objectives and constraints with fewer plug-in routine calls in the convex case.

paragraphs: Deep networks trained on noisy annotations can initially learn from correctly labeled examples before eventually memorizing incorrect labels. This paper investigates that progression and uses the early phase as a resource for robust classification. The authors prove that early learning and later memorization occur in high-dimensional classification even with simple linear models, and explain them theoretically in that setting.

The proposed method preserves useful early predictions through regularization. It first uses techniques from semi-supervised learning to construct target probabilities from model outputs. A regularization term then steers subsequent training toward these targets, implicitly preventing memorization of false labels.

This approach differs from using early predictions primarily to identify clean examples and discard or correct the rest. Here, the early learning signal directly shapes continued optimization. On several standard benchmarks and real-world datasets, the framework demonstrates robustness to noisy annotations and results comparable to the state of the art. The contribution connects a theoretical account of training dynamics with a practical mechanism for retaining their useful early behavior.
neurips-2020-early-learning-regularizati.tldr: Early-learning regularization uses targets derived from model predictions to resist memorizing incorrect training labels.

paragraphs: A graph edge can hide several kinds of relationships between the same entities. In a social network, for example, a connection might represent friendship, a working relationship, or both. Treating every connection as a single undifferentiated relation leaves those underlying distinctions entangled when a graph neural network aggregates information.

FactorGCN takes a simple graph and separates it into several factorized graphs, each representing a latent relationship among nodes. It then aggregates node features separately within the corresponding latent spaces. The resulting features are intended to preserve distinctions between relationships rather than combining all connected information in one shared aggregation.

The authors evaluate the model qualitatively and quantitatively on synthetic and real-world datasets. They report encouraging results for separating relations and aggregating features, together with improved downstream performance. These findings support learning relational structure that is not explicitly labeled in the input graph. The method's central contribution is to make that inferred structure part of how node representations are constructed.
neurips-2020-factorizable-graph-convolut.tldr: FactorGCN separates graph connections into latent relation types and aggregates features within each to improve learned representations.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks combine information from node features and connections, but both sources can be targeted by adversarial changes. This paper introduces the Graph Information Bottleneck principle to balance useful representation power with robustness. Its aim is a representation that retains the information needed for a task while limiting retained information about the input.

The formulation maximizes mutual information between the representation and the target while constraining mutual information between the representation and the input data. Its graph-specific contribution is to regularize structural information as well as feature information. The authors design two sampling algorithms for structural regularization and build two models, GIB-Cat and GIB-Bern.

Experiments test resilience to attacks on graph structure and node features. The proposed models outperform state-of-the-art graph defense models in the reported evaluation, with empirical improvements reaching up to 31%. That figure describes the reported experimental gains rather than a uniform guarantee. The results support applying the information bottleneck to both components of graph data when learning representations intended to withstand adversarial perturbations.
neurips-2020-graph-information-bottlenec.tldr: Graph Information Bottleneck regularizes both graph structure and node features to learn task-relevant representations with improved empirical adversarial robustness.

paragraphs: Adversarial attacks serve two connected purposes: testing whether a defense is robust and supplying difficult examples for robust training. A common attack maximizes a classification loss within an allowed constraint set using projected gradient descent. This paper modifies that optimization objective to make the gradient directions more useful for finding adversarial inputs.

The authors add a relaxation term to a standard loss and introduce Guided Adversarial Margin Attack, or GAMA. GAMA uses the model's mapping of the clean image to guide adversary generation. The proposed guidance produces stronger attacks, and evaluations against multiple defenses show improved attack performance relative to existing attacks.

The same relaxation term also supports Guided Adversarial Training, or GAT, where it is used in attack generation and training. The authors report more efficient adversarial training and state-of-the-art performance among single-step defenses. Together, the two methods show how modifying the attack objective can strengthen defense evaluation while also improving the procedure used to train a robust model.
neurips-2020-guided-adversarial-attack-f.tldr: A clean-image-guided relaxation strengthens adversarial attacks and supports improved single-step adversarial training.

paragraphs: The Sparse Vector Technique is a foundational tool in differential privacy and a component of algorithms for adaptive data analysis and model-agnostic private learning. Improving this building block can therefore matter beyond a single application. This paper revisits its privacy analysis using Rényi differential privacy and develops new privacy bounds, theoretical insights, and algorithm variants.

A central variant replaces the standard Laplace mechanism with a Gaussian mechanism. The authors attribute its better utility to more concentrated noise and tighter composition, meaning a sharper accounting of privacy when mechanisms are combined. The contribution thus joins a change in the noise mechanism with a privacy analysis that better captures its behavior.

Extensive empirical evaluation supports the advantages of Gaussian SVT over Laplace SVT and other alternatives. The authors suggest that substituting it into existing SVT-based algorithms could help make downstream tasks practical. This downstream benefit is presented as a possibility motivated by the evaluations; the directly reported evidence concerns the Gaussian variant's utility and comparative empirical performance.
neurips-2020-improving-sparse-vector-tec.tldr: Rényi differential privacy yields improved Sparse Vector Technique analyses and a Gaussian variant with better reported utility.

paragraphs: Profile maximum likelihood, or PML, is an important ingredient in estimating symmetric properties of distributions. This paper develops an efficient approximation algorithm whose performance can benefit from the structure of the observed instance. It matches the previous best efficient algorithms and improves when the observations contain only a small number of distinct frequencies.

The algorithm exploits a newly identified sparsity structure in approximate PML distributions. It also uses a new matrix rounding algorithm, which the authors present as independently useful. These ingredients provide the first provably computationally efficient implementation of PseudoPML, a general framework for estimating a broad class of symmetric properties.

The authors further obtain efficient PML-based estimators for distributions with small profile entropy, using that quantity as an instance-based complexity measure. They also develop a simpler, more practical PseudoPML implementation that matches the best known theoretical guarantees for such an estimator and evaluate it empirically. The overall contribution is to connect computational efficiency with specific structure in the estimation problem, rather than treating all instances identically.
neurips-2020-instance-based-approximatio.tldr: New sparsity and rounding techniques make approximate PML computation more efficient on structured instances and enable provably efficient PseudoPML.

paragraphs: Single-image super-resolution reconstructs a higher-resolution image from a lower-resolution input. Deep learning has improved reconstruction quality, but balancing that quality against model complexity remains a challenge. LAPAR addresses this tradeoff by changing the form of the prediction problem, using a structured representation for the image transformation.

Instead of learning the low-to-high-resolution mapping directly, the network predicts linear coefficients over a dictionary of predefined filter bases. These coefficients allow the filters to be assembled adaptively for individual pixels. Learning how to combine an existing set of bases provides a more constrained parameterization of the restoration operation.

The authors report that this representation produces a lightweight model that is easy to optimize while achieving state-of-the-art results on super-resolution benchmarks. They also extend the same idea to image denoising and JPEG deblocking, with strong reported performance. These extensions show that predicting combinations of predefined filters can support several restoration tasks, beyond the super-resolution problem that motivates the architecture.
neurips-2020-lapar-linearly-assembled-pi.tldr: LAPAR predicts pixel-adaptive combinations of predefined filters to deliver lightweight, high-quality super-resolution and other image restoration.

paragraphs: Controlling sentence structure requires a text generator to represent more than the words it produces. This paper explores learning hidden templates inside a structured variational autoencoder, so the model can infer sentence organization during training and use it to guide generation. The training challenge is how to learn through the structured choices that define those templates.

The proposed Gumbel-CRF replaces discrete CRF sampling with a soft, continuous relaxation. It does this through a relaxed version of Forward-Filtering Backward-Sampling. This allows reparameterized gradient estimation, giving the training process a way to adjust the model through relaxed structured samples.

The authors report more stable gradients than score-function estimators and show that the inference network learns interpretable templates. Those templates allow control of the decoder at test time. Experiments on data-to-text generation and unsupervised paraphrase generation demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The contribution combines a training mechanism for structured latent variables with a practical use for those variables: controlling how generated sentences are organized.
neurips-2020-latent-template-induction-w.tldr: Gumbel-CRFs enable stable training of structured latent sentence templates that can control text generation.

paragraphs: A pretrained language model contains knowledge in its parameters, but its ability to reason with that knowledge can be difficult to control. Earlier reasoning demonstrations used explicit facts under a closed-world assumption. This paper asks whether training can teach a model to combine knowledge already encoded during pretraining with new statements supplied in natural language.

The authors introduce a procedure that automatically generates datasets for teaching reasoning skills. They demonstrate inference involving implicit taxonomic and world knowledge, chaining, and counting. The central contribution is a demonstration that systematic reasoning can draw on both stored knowledge and explicitly provided statements within the same task.

The trained models also generalize beyond the training distribution by combining multiple reasoning skills in individual examples. This supports the possibility of teaching reusable reasoning behavior, rather than only performance on the training combinations. The authors envision open-domain systems that users could correct by adding natural-language statements. That interactive, continually improving system is a future direction motivated by the demonstrated reasoning results.
neurips-2020-leap-of-thought-teaching-pr.tldr: Automatically generated training data teaches language models to combine implicit knowledge with explicit statements and compose reasoning skills.

paragraphs: Many theoretical results about neural-network learning concern problems that linear methods can also solve. Such results establish useful capabilities but leave open why learning a nonlinear representation can offer a computational advantage. This paper addresses that gap by studying sparse parity functions as a learning problem with an inherently nonlinear aspect.

The authors show that, under certain data distributions, gradient descent can learn sparse parities using a depth-two neural network. Their comparison uses the same distributions: linear methods cannot efficiently learn those parities there. The relevant linear approach is a classifier built on a representation of examples that is fixed independently of the data.

The result provides a theoretical separation between the specified neural-network training procedure and linear methods in this setting. Its force comes from comparing learnability under shared distributions, rather than changing the data between approaches. The distribution condition is essential to the stated result: the paper establishes a particular setting where neural learning goes beyond linear methods, not unrestricted learnability of sparse parities.
neurips-2020-learning-parities-with-neur.tldr: Under certain distributions, gradient descent learns sparse parities with a depth-two network while linear methods cannot learn them efficiently.

paragraphs: Pruning reduces model size by removing weights. Magnitude pruning is widely used in supervised learning, but the authors find it less effective when a pretrained model is being adapted through fine-tuning. This paper develops a pruning approach intended to respond more effectively to that transfer-learning setting, which is important for large language models.

Movement pruning is a simple, deterministic first-order method. It uses information associated with fine-tuning to make pruning more adaptive, rather than relying only on weight magnitude. The authors provide mathematical foundations and compare the approach with existing zeroth-order and first-order pruning methods.

Experiments on large pretrained language models show significant improvements when the resulting networks are highly sparse. Combined with distillation, the method retains as little as 3% of model parameters with minimal reported accuracy loss. The distillation condition is part of that strongest compression result. Overall, the findings support designing pruning criteria around adaptation during fine-tuning when aggressively compressing a pretrained model.
neurips-2020-movement-pruning-adaptive-s.tldr: Movement pruning adapts weight removal to pretrained-model fine-tuning and, with distillation, retains just 3% of parameters with minimal reported accuracy loss.

paragraphs: Self-supervised denoising learns from individual noisy images, avoiding the need for clean target images in that training framework. Many existing approaches share a theoretical foundation that requires a property called J-invariance. The authors analyze that foundation and argue that both the theory and the restriction may reduce denoising performance.

Noise2Same introduces a different training objective by deriving a self-supervised upper bound on the usual supervised loss. This gives the model a loss that can be optimized using noisy images while remaining linked to the supervised denoising objective. The framework requires neither J-invariance nor additional information about the noise model.

The authors study Noise2Same theoretically and experimentally, reporting substantial improvements over previous self-supervised denoising methods in both restoration performance and training efficiency. Removing the stated restrictions also allows a wider range of denoising applications. The contribution is the connection between a new self-supervised bound and a training framework that relaxes a constraint the authors identify as potentially detrimental.
neurips-2020-noise2same-optimizing-a-sel.tldr: Noise2Same trains denoisers through a self-supervised upper bound without requiring J-invariance or extra noise-model information.

paragraphs: An online learner may face two ways of judging the same decisions. The paper's hiring example distinguishes a recruiter's treatment of errors from applicants' greater concern about false negatives. It asks whether combining expert advice can achieve low regret on a primary loss while performing little worse than even the worst expert on a secondary loss.

The authors show that this goal is impossible without a bounded-variance assumption on the secondary loss. They then study the more general goal of controlling primary regret while keeping secondary loss within a linear threshold. This separates the desired performance on the main objective from a bound on the additional cost.

A positive result applies when every expert exceeds the secondary threshold by only o(T) on any time interval: any switching-limited algorithm can achieve the goal. When some experts violate that assumption, the proposed algorithms require external oracles that decide when experts should be deactivated and reactivated. The findings identify conditions and additional information that make simultaneous loss control possible.
neurips-2020-online-learning-with-primar.tldr: The paper establishes when online learners can control a secondary loss while maintaining low primary regret, and when that goal is impossible.

paragraphs: This paper studies online prediction of binary matrix entries using side information. It provides an algorithm with mistake and regret guarantees, with the mistake bound taking the form O(D/gamma^2) up to logarithmic factors. The two quantities separate the role of side information from the difficulty associated with a classification margin.

The margin gamma is defined through factorizations of the underlying matrix into PQ^T. Rows of P act as classifiers, and rows of Q act as instances. Gamma is the largest normalized margin among factorizations consistent with observed entries. The quasi-dimension D captures the quality of the available side information.

Without useful side information, D equals m+n for an m-by-n matrix. In an ideal case where that information predicts the underlying factors, D can scale with k+l, the numbers of distinct row and column factors. The authors also extend the algorithm to an inductive setting and give an example with D bounded by O(k^2+l^2), where side information is not directly specified beforehand.
neurips-2020-online-matrix-completion-wi.tldr: An online binary matrix completion algorithm gains stronger mistake bounds when side information predicts the matrix's latent factor structure.

paragraphs: Finding approximate Nash equilibria is difficult in large zero-sum games where players lack complete information. Policy Space Response Oracles, or PSRO, has a convergence guarantee, but training a reinforcement-learning policy at every iteration makes it slow. The authors also show through counterexamples and experiments that two scaling approaches, DCH and Rectified PSRO, can fail to converge even in small games.

Pipeline PSRO organizes reinforcement-learning workers into a hierarchy. Each worker trains against policies generated at lower levels, allowing training to proceed in parallel while retaining convergence guarantees. This pipeline is the mechanism used to connect increased computational parallelism with equilibrium finding.

Across several imperfect-information games, the authors show convergence to an approximate Nash equilibrium and faster convergence with more parallel workers. They also introduce an open-source Barrage Stratego environment, whose approximate game-tree complexity is 10^50. P2SRO achieves state-of-the-art performance there and beats all existing bots in the reported results, demonstrating the method on a particularly large game.
neurips-2020-pipeline-psro-a-scalable-ap.tldr: Pipeline PSRO parallelizes policy training through a hierarchy while preserving approximate-equilibrium convergence and improving speed in evaluated games.

paragraphs: Compressing a trained model changes its weights through operations such as quantization or pruning. This paper proposes making the weights more compatible with compression during optimization. Its position-based scaled gradient, or PSG, rescales the gradient according to the current position of the weight vector.

The authors prove that gradient descent using PSG is equivalent to ordinary gradient descent in a transformed weight space. That space is constructed through an appropriately designed invertible mapping of the original weights. This gives a theoretical interpretation of the update rule as optimization in a different geometry.

Empirically, PSG acts as a regularizer that narrows the gap between the weight distributions of full-precision and compressed models. The authors evaluate pruning and quantization on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, reporting effectiveness even at extremely low bit widths. The intended deployment benefit is flexibility: a model can be used in either uncompressed or compressed form according to available resources. The results support shaping optimization itself to make those modes more compatible.
neurips-2020-position-based-scaled-gradi.tldr: Position-based gradient scaling makes learned weights more compatible with pruning and quantization, supporting compressed and uncompressed deployment.

paragraphs: Computer-vision networks can require substantial working memory because their intermediate activation maps are large. Rapidly shrinking those maps helps memory usage, but ordinary pooling or strided convolutions can lose accuracy when they aggregate too coarsely. RNNPool addresses this tradeoff with a pooling operator based on recurrent neural networks.

The operator aggregates features over large image patches and quickly downsamples activation maps. Experiments indicate that a single RNNPool layer can replace multiple blocks in architectures including MobileNets and DenseNet. The evaluated tasks include image classification and face detection.

The authors report significant reductions in computational complexity and peak inference memory while retaining comparable accuracy. They also combine RNNPool with the S3FD architecture to build a face detector for ARM Cortex-M4-class microcontrollers using under 256 KB of RAM, reporting state-of-the-art mean average precision for that setting. The contribution targets the memory needed during computation, showing how a learned aggregation operator can make vision inference feasible under a tight working-memory budget.
neurips-2020-rnnpool-efficient-non-linea.tldr: RNNPool uses recurrent networks to downsample image features efficiently, reducing inference memory and computation while retaining comparable accuracy.

paragraphs: Pruning is often understood as using training data to discover a particularly effective smaller network. This paper tests that interpretation for several recent unstructured pruning methods, focusing on methods that select subnetworks from randomly initialized networks. The authors call these selected subnetworks initial tickets.

Their sanity checks find that a set of these methods makes little use of training-data information. They also find that randomly changing which weights survive within each layer leaves final performance unaffected, provided each layer retains the same number of weights. These findings point to the importance of layerwise pruning ratios in the examined methods.

Motivated by this result, the authors choose simple data-independent ratios and randomly prune each layer to create random tickets. Experiments show that these zero-shot selections match or outperform existing initial tickets. One existing method does pass the sanity checks; combining it with the random-ticket ratios produces hybrid tickets with further improvements. The evidence challenges specific pruning methods' presumed mechanisms while also supplying simpler alternatives.
neurips-2020-sanity-checking-pruning-met.tldr: Sanity checks reveal that several initial-ticket pruning methods gain little from data or exact weight selection, motivating competitive random pruning.

paragraphs: This paper studies the computational difficulty of learning a halfspace classifier that remains reliable under adversarial input perturbations. It considers proper learning, meaning the learned classifier must itself be a halfspace. The setting is distribution-independent and agnostic, so the learning formulation does not assume a particular data distribution or perfectly consistent labels.

The analysis focuses on perturbations measured using L_p norms. The authors provide a computationally efficient learning algorithm together with a nearly matching computational hardness result. These complementary results describe both what an algorithm can achieve and the computational obstacles to improving on it within the studied problem.

A central implication is that L_infinity perturbations are provably computationally harder to handle than L_p perturbations with finite p at least two. The way adversarial changes are measured therefore affects the difficulty of robust learning, even within the same classifier family and learning framework. The contribution is a theoretical comparison of perturbation regimes, supported by an algorithm and a closely aligned hardness result.
neurips-2020-the-complexity-of-adversari.tldr: Algorithmic and hardness results show that robust proper halfspace learning is computationally harder for L_infinity perturbations than for finite L_p norms with p at least two.
